core_idea: Computing modelled on permaculture: care for the Earth, care for people and fair shares, applied to hardware, software and networks, with refusal ('not doing') as a first option.
who_governs: No owner; a community of practice and working group that publishes principles and leaves practice to situated local groups.
enforcer: None formal; norms are enforced socially within the community, and the wiki says permacomputing is 'an anti-capitalist political project'.
limits: Treats limits as the design starting point: planetary boundaries, finite chips and e-waste, intermittent energy; systems should tolerate interruption and need not run 24/7; cites the Jevons paradox against efficiency-only answers.
ai_governance: Would begin with 'Observe first' and 'Not doing': ask whether the task needs a frontier model at all, refuse scaling for its own sake, expose energy and hardware costs ('expose the seams'), extend hardware life and run compute only when renewable energy is available.
example: Solar Protocol: a website served from whichever solar-powered server in a volunteer network has the most sunshine; pages drop to low resolution when batteries run low.
strongest_criticism: It has no institution able to govern a large system and no account of who decides for people who want more compute; at frontier scale it is a stance of refusal, not a governance design.

core_idea: Meet the needs of all people within the means of the living planet: a social foundation no one should fall below and an ecological ceiling humanity should not overshoot.
who_governs: Whoever adopts it (cities, firms, governments); DEAL, the Doughnut Economics Action Lab, curates practice and sets 'principles of practice'.
enforcer: No enforcer in the framework itself; enforcement comes only when an adopter writes it into law, budgets or charters.
limits: Explicit two-sided limit: nine planetary boundaries form the ceiling, twelve social needs the floor; 'aim to thrive rather than to grow'.
ai_governance: Would count compute against the ceiling (energy, water, materials, land) and judge it by whether it lifts people above the floor; DEAL's organisational design layers (purpose, networks, governance, ownership, finance) would apply to the firm.
example: Amsterdam adopted the City Doughnut as a policy framework in April 2020 to guide its post-pandemic recovery and circular-economy strategy.
strongest_criticism: It is a dashboard, not a mechanism: it names the safe and just space but supplies no rule for allocating the ceiling among people or nations, and adoption has not yet bound a city's growth decisions.

core_idea: High-income economies should abandon GDP growth as a goal and plan a reduction of energy and material throughput while securing human needs and well-being.
who_governs: Democratic states and planning processes; degrowth scholars stress participatory deliberation over which production is 'destructive and unnecessary'.
enforcer: Governments through law, budgets and public provision; no non-state enforcer.
limits: The core claim is that limits bind now: decoupling GDP from resource use has not been fast enough, so throughput must fall in rich countries, freeing energy and materials for low- and middle-income countries.
ai_governance: Would treat frontier compute as a candidate for 'unnecessary' production unless it demonstrably serves needs; would cap or ration energy and materials for data centres in rich countries and decide democratically what AI is for.
example: No government has adopted degrowth; the nearest practice is in policies degrowth scholars cite, such as Vienna's public housing (Hickel et al., Nature 2022).
strongest_criticism: Critics argue that slowing growth risks unemployment and poverty, especially for the poorest, and that green growth through decoupling is possible; there is no working national case.

core_idea: An economy designed to serve people and planet, with success measured by shared wellbeing rather than GDP growth, steered by four principles: predistribution, purpose, prevention and people-powered decisions.
who_governs: Governments (the Wellbeing Economy Governments partnership: Scotland, Iceland, New Zealand, Wales, Finland, with Canada participating) and the WEAll alliance of organisations.
enforcer: Governments through budgets and statute; in Wales a Future Generations Commissioner holds public bodies to account.
limits: Treats limits through 'prevention' and planetary wellbeing indicators; less explicit about hard caps than the doughnut or degrowth.
ai_governance: Would judge AI by its effect on wellbeing indicators and prevent harm before it occurs; citizen assemblies and participatory budgeting would decide public investment in AI.
example: New Zealand's 2019 Wellbeing Budget allocated spending against wellbeing priorities, including NZ$2 billion for mental health.
strongest_criticism: It changes the measure more than the outcome: reviews of New Zealand's budgets asked what really changed, and a change of government in 2023-24 moved away from the framing, showing how easily it is reversed.

core_idea: Communities can govern a shared resource sustainably without either privatisation or state control when they meet design conditions such as clear boundaries, rules fitted to local conditions, participation in rule-making, monitoring, graduated sanctions and conflict resolution.
who_governs: The users of the resource, through collective-choice arrangements nested in larger polycentric governance.
enforcer: The community itself: monitors accountable to users and graduated sanctions; external authorities must recognise the community's right to organise.
limits: Limits are the reason the institution exists: appropriation rules are fitted to what the resource can sustain over generations.
ai_governance: Would treat compute, data or model weights as a common-pool resource governed by those who contribute and depend on it, with monitoring of use and sanctions for overuse; polycentric layers for global effects.
example: Swiss alpine pastures and Spanish huerta irrigation systems governed for centuries, documented in Governing the Commons (1990) and Ostrom's 2009 Nobel lecture.
strongest_criticism: The principles were drawn from small, bounded, long-lived communities; frontier AI's users and affected people are global, anonymous and fast-changing, which is the case the principles fit worst.

core_idea: Large numbers of people cooperate over the internet to produce shared goods without market prices or managerial hierarchy as the main coordination (Benkler).
who_governs: Contributors through project governance (foundations, elected councils, maintainers).
enforcer: Licences (copyleft) and project communities; foundations hold trademarks.
limits: Treats digital goods as non-rival, so it says little about physical limits; the energy and hardware beneath it are outside its frame.
ai_governance: Would produce open models, open datasets and open evaluations as shared goods; governance by contributors and licence terms.
example: Wikipedia and Linux; Debian has governed itself through a constitution and developer votes without a legal entity.
strongest_criticism: It depends on unpaid labour and skews towards those with time and money to contribute; and open release of frontier weights moves misuse risk onto the public with no one able to recall them.

core_idea: An enterprise owned and democratically controlled by its members (workers, users or producers), one member one vote.
who_governs: Members through a general assembly electing a board.
enforcer: Members, and cooperative law in many jurisdictions; the ICA principles are the shared standard.
limits: No inherent ecological limit; cooperatives can grow and pollute; the limit is on extraction by outside capital.
ai_governance: A cooperative AI lab would answer to its members; who the members are (workers, users, affected communities) decides whose interests count.
example: Mondragon: 81 self-governing cooperatives with about 70,000 people in the Basque Country.
strongest_criticism: Members' interests are not the public's: worker or user co-ops can externalise harm as readily as investor-owned firms, and capital-intensive sectors are hard to finance without outside investors (Fagor Electrodomésticos, a Mondragon cooperative, went bankrupt in 2013).

core_idea: Digital platforms owned and governed by the people who depend on them, usually workers or users, instead of venture investors.
who_governs: Worker or user members.
enforcer: Members; the Platform Cooperativism Consortium (The New School) supports the field.
limits: None specific beyond those of cooperatives.
ai_governance: An AI platform owned by its data workers or users, who would set pay, labelling conditions and deployment rules.
example: The Drivers Cooperative in New York City, a driver-owned ride-hail and paratransit company.
strongest_criticism: Most struggle to raise capital and reach scale against investor-backed rivals (e2c.how records failures such as Ampled and Juno); frontier AI needs billions in capital the model cannot raise.

core_idea: Control stays with people tied to the company's mission ('self-determination') and profits serve the purpose rather than owners ('purpose orientation'), locked in legally, often through a foundation or trust holding the voting shares.
who_governs: Stewards who hold voting rights but cannot sell them or take the profits; in Patagonia's case the Patagonia Purpose Trust, guided by the Chouinard family.
enforcer: The trust or foundation, through its voting stock; and the legal lock on transfer and profit extraction.
limits: Limits extraction and sale, not resource use; Patagonia states the tension between growth and environmental impact remains.
ai_governance: A frontier lab whose voting shares sit with a purpose trust that cannot sell to an acquirer or pay out to investors; the trust approves board seats and charter changes.
example: Patagonia (2022): 100% of voting stock to the Patagonia Purpose Trust, 100% of non-voting stock to the Holdfast Collective; also Bosch, Zeiss, Novo Nordisk.
strongest_criticism: The purpose is guarded by a small, often family-selected group with no duty to the people affected; the trust protects the mission from investors, not from its own stewards.

core_idea: A non-charitable trust that owns a company for a stated purpose in perpetuity, with an enforcer named in the trust deed (US perpetual purpose trusts in Oregon and Delaware law).
who_governs: Trustees and a trust protector or committee, often including workers and community.
enforcer: A named enforcer under the trust instrument, who can sue the trustees.
limits: Perpetual time horizon by design; resource limits only if written into the purpose.
ai_governance: A lab owned by a purpose trust whose deed names AI safety and public benefit and names an enforcer outside the company.
example: Patagonia's Purpose Trust is the best-known case; Purpose Foundation advises others on the model.
strongest_criticism: The enforcer is chosen by the founders, and perpetual purposes cannot easily adapt; whether courts will police vague purposes is largely untested.

core_idea: Instead of selling to an acquirer or listing on a stock market, a startup transfers ownership and control to the community it serves: users, workers or a mix.
who_governs: The community after the transition (co-op members, an employee trust, a DAO or a foundation).
enforcer: Depends on the vehicle chosen; the community's ownership rights.
limits: None specific; the limit is on investor extraction at exit.
ai_governance: An AI firm would plan its 'exit' to users, workers and affected communities rather than to public markets.
example: The WELL forum (sold in 2012 to an entity of 11 long-time users); Defector Media (worker-owned); Namaste Solar (worker co-op, about $40m revenue in 2023).
strongest_criticism: The e2c.how case list records as many failures and ambiguous outcomes as successes; founders often keep key infrastructure, and tokenised versions concentrate control.

model: Public utility and public option for compute
core_idea: AI infrastructure (compute, data, models) built and run as public goods with universal access, public accountability and permanent public ownership, alongside private providers.
who_governs: Public institutions: governments, public universities, national labs; accountable through elected officials.
enforcer: Legislatures and public-law accountability (freedom of information, audit, elections).
limits: Not inherently limit-aware; a public option can also scale; the gain is that scale becomes a public decision.
ai_governance: Public compute clusters and open public models, with access rules set in public; the Public AI Network calls for public investment at each layer of the stack and vertically integrated public utilities.
example: Apertus, a fully open multilingual model released in 2025 by EPFL, ETH Zurich and the Swiss National Supercomputing Centre, served through the Public AI Inference Utility.
strongest_criticism: Governments may be slower, less safety-competent and more politically captured than firms; a state with frontier capability raises its own misuse and surveillance risks.

core_idea: Independent trustees steward data for a stated purpose and the beneficiaries' interests, deciding who may access it, for what and to whose benefit.
who_governs: Trustees under a governance document.
enforcer: Trustees, who take on duties and some liabilities; the ODI notes data trusts 'are not legal trusts' in the strict sense.
limits: Limits on use and access, not on resources.
ai_governance: Training data held in trusts whose trustees license it to developers on terms set for the data subjects' benefit, with power to refuse.
example: The ODI ran three data-trust pilots in 2018-19 with the UK Office for AI and Innovate UK.
strongest_criticism: The pilots found no case ready to run; trustees' duties are unclear in law and the people whose data it is rarely choose the trustees.

core_idea: People pool their personal data in a member-owned cooperative and decide together, or case by case, who may use it.
who_governs: Members, through the cooperative's democratic governance.
enforcer: Members.
limits: Limits on use set by members; no resource limits.
ai_governance: A data co-op would license members' data for training only on terms members vote for, and share returns.
example: MIDATA, a Swiss health-data cooperative whose account holders grant selective access for research and can become members who control it.
strongest_criticism: Membership stays small, data's value comes from aggregation across many who never join, and co-ops cannot govern data scraped without them.

core_idea: A nonprofit holds land in trust for a community permanently and leases it, keeping housing or other uses affordable and out of speculation.
who_governs: A board usually split among residents, wider community members and public representatives.
enforcer: The trust through the ground lease, and its members.
limits: Permanent time horizon on land use; removes land from the market.
ai_governance: Data-centre land, water and power could be held by a community trust that leases them on terms the host community sets, including the right not to renew.
example: Champlain Housing Trust, Vermont, founded 1984 by the City of Burlington; the largest US community land trust.
strongest_criticism: It caps resale gains for residents and depends on public subsidy to acquire land; it governs a site, not a supply chain or a global technology.

core_idea: Design out waste and pollution, keep products and materials in use at their highest value, and regenerate natural systems.
who_governs: Firms and governments that adopt it; promoted by the Ellen MacArthur Foundation and EU policy.
enforcer: Regulators through product, waste and right-to-repair law.
limits: Addresses material loops; does not set a ceiling on total throughput.
ai_governance: Would extend server and chip life, design for repair and recover materials; demand for compute is left as given.
example: EU circular economy action plan; Amsterdam's circular strategy alongside its City Doughnut.
strongest_criticism: Critics find unclear limits, thermodynamic barriers to closing loops and rebound effects, where recycled supply adds to rather than replaces primary production (Corvellec, Stowell and Johansson, 2022).

core_idea: The economy is a living system and should follow the principles that keep living systems healthy (right relationship, holistic wealth, balance, circulation, empowered participation), leaving the whole stronger.
who_governs: Not specified; addressed to investors, firms and communities (Capital Institute).
enforcer: None formal.
limits: Treats limits as health conditions of a living system; the economy must sit in 'right relationship' with the biosphere.
ai_governance: Would ask whether AI development strengthens or drains the communities and ecosystems it draws on, and would measure wealth beyond money.
example: Capital Institute's field guide cases; regenerative agriculture is the most developed practice.
strongest_criticism: It is a set of principles without enforcement or measurement standards, so 'regenerative' is easily claimed by firms that change little.

core_idea: Enterprises and organisations (co-ops, associations, mutuals, foundations, social enterprises) with a social or public purpose, based on voluntary cooperation, democratic governance and primacy of people over capital in distributing surplus.
who_governs: Members and democratic governance within each organisation; recognised by the UN General Assembly (A/RES/77/281, April 2023) and the ILO (2022).
enforcer: Members; states through enabling law.
limits: Not explicit about ecological limits; limits are on profit distribution.
ai_governance: AI built and deployed by SSE organisations, with surplus reinvested in purpose and governance by members.
example: UN General Assembly resolution 77/281 (2023) recognising the SSE for sustainable development; national SSE laws in several countries.
strongest_criticism: It is a broad umbrella whose organisations are mostly small; recognition has not brought capital or a path to running capital-intensive technology.

core_idea: A good life lived in harmony with community and nature, drawn from Andean Indigenous thought; nature is a subject with rights, not a resource.
who_governs: In Ecuador, the state under the 2008 constitution; communities and anyone may act for nature.
enforcer: Courts: Ecuador's constitution lets any person demand that authorities enforce the rights of nature.
limits: Nature has the right to exist, persist and regenerate its cycles; limits are owed to nature itself.
ai_governance: Would give the ecosystems that supply energy, water and minerals for compute standing to be defended in court, and judge AI by its contribution to collective good living.
example: Ecuador's 2008 constitution recognises rights of nature (Pachamama); courts have applied it, and voters chose in 2023 to keep Yasuní oil underground.
strongest_criticism: The state that wrote it into the constitution kept funding itself from oil and mining; a 2025 constitutional rewrite proposal put the rights of nature at risk.

core_idea: 'A person is a person through other persons': personhood and the good are relational, so harm to the community is harm to each member.
who_governs: Communities, through consensus and relational obligations rather than individual rights alone.
enforcer: No formal enforcer; proposed as a basis for AI ethics and human-rights frameworks.
limits: Time horizon includes ancestors and descendants; limits come from obligations to community.
ai_governance: Would judge AI by how it affects relationships and the most excluded, and challenge governance built on individual rationality and consent (Mhlambi, 2020).
example: South Africa's constitutional court has drawn on ubuntu in its jurisprudence; applied to AI governance in Mhlambi's 2020 Carr Center paper.
strongest_criticism: It is an ethic, not a governance mechanism, and its communal emphasis can be invoked to override individual dissent.

core_idea: Indigenous Peoples have the right to control data about their peoples, lands and knowledge: Collective benefit, Authority to control, Responsibility and Ethics.
who_governs: Indigenous nations and their own institutions (GIDA, the Global Indigenous Data Alliance, set out the principles in 2019).
enforcer: Indigenous governance bodies, licences and the communities themselves; national law recognises it unevenly.
limits: Intergenerational: data and knowledge are held for future generations; limits on use are set by the people.
ai_governance: Indigenous data and language could not be used for training without consent and benefit; licences would bind downstream use.
example: Te Hiku Media built te reo Māori speech recognition on community recordings hosted on its own platform under its Kaitiakitanga licence, rather than uploading them to big-tech platforms.
strongest_criticism: It protects a people's data but not the global commons of scraped text; enforcement against foreign developers depends on licences and goodwill that are hard to police.

model: Benefit corporations and public benefit corporations (contrast)
core_idea: A for-profit corporation that must balance stockholders' pecuniary interests, the best interests of those materially affected by its conduct and a stated public benefit.
who_governs: The board of directors, elected by stockholders.
enforcer: Only stockholders holding at least 2% of shares (or $2m in listed shares) may sue to enforce the balance; directors owe no duty to any person on account of the public benefit.
limits: No limits; growth and capital raising are unchanged.
ai_governance: This is Anthropic's structure: the board balances, the Long-Term Benefit Trust elects some directors, and the affected cannot enforce.
example: Anthropic PBC; Patagonia was a California benefit corporation before its steward-ownership transfer.
strongest_criticism: The purpose binds only as far as stockholders choose to enforce it; the people it names as beneficiaries have no standing (Del. Code tit. 8, §§ 365, 367).
